newsitem.title: USA: Police patrol streets of riot-torn Florida city.
newsitem.headline: Police patrol streets of riot-torn Florida city.

text.p: An uneasy calm returned to the streets of St. Petersburg on Friday after a night of rioting in a mainly black neighbourhood sparked by the police killing of a black motorist.
Hundreds of police, some in riot gear, continued to patrol a section of the city but rioters had dispersed before dawn and the police chief said the streets were safe.

Police chief Darrell Stephens told an early-morning news conference that at least 28 fires had been set by arsonists during the rioting, 11 people including seven police officers were injured and 20 people had been arrested.
He said police presence in the south St. Petersburg neighbourhood would be stepped up and the situation monitored on an hourly basis for the rest of the day.
"There's calm on the streets right now and we think it is going to stay that way. There will be an increased police presence but it is safe to walk the streets," he said at 6:30 a.m. EDT (1030 GMT).
"We are going to continue throughout the day and the evening with a stepped up presence of police officers on the street to handle any difficulties that may arise," added Stephens.
He refused to discuss the incident which sparked the riots, saying the state attorney's office was investigating the shooting and it was "inappropriate to speculate what took place".
Police initially said the incident began when two officers, a white male and white female, stopped a car for speeding in a neighbourhood with a history of trouble with drug dealers.

They shot the motorist because they believed he was trying to run them down after his gold Pontiac lurched forward, police said. But some witnesses said the driver had done nothing to prompt the shooting.
"She shot him for nothing, nothing," Rachel Wilson, who witnessed the traffic stop, told St. Petersburg television station WTOG.

The riot began shortly afterward at the intersection where the shooting took place. The crowd began to throw rocks and bottles at police, and scattered rioting quickly spread over several blocks as word of the shooting spread.
More than 150 firefighters from 11 fire departments responded to 89 night calls during the night as rioters threw Molotov cocktails, and a taskforce of arson investigators has been assembled.

Police spokeswoman Lilla Davis said that during the night as many as 500 police officers were deployed in the city to quell the rioting and that by 3:30 a.m. EDT (0730 GMT) the situation was under control.
The disturbances began about 7:30 p.m. EDT (1130 GMT) on Thursday at the intersection of 18th Avenue and 16th Street South and stretched across several blocks.
St. Petersburg Mayor David Fischer said city officials would meet with black community leaders on Friday morning to try to prevent a recurrence of violence and to discuss grievances.

"These things are spontaneous, it just ignites," said Fischer. "It's a wake-up call that you have a lot of work to do. We will be meeting with our local leaders preparing to keep it calm for the rest of the day and tonight."
The parking lot near where the shooting took place used to be the centre of the crack and cocaine trade, officials said.

Tensions ran high in the area during police crackdowns on the drug trade in the late 1980s and early 1990s. But they were thought to have improved after Police Chief Ernest Curtsinger, who was viewed by blacks as hostile to them, was removed in 1992 and the current police chief, Darrel Stephens, was credited with healing the wounds.
